utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand you wish to say something in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. It has nothing to do with the witness. A few minutes ago, I received your ruling. I see that you made the ruling yesterday refusing my request to go for treatment, medical treatment. I should like to tell you that I consider this a highly unjust decision, because your assertions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing -- I'm not hearing any comments on that. I'm not receiving any comments on that. If that is what you have to say, we'll call the witness. Please call the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I want it to remain on the record that I demand that the Appeals Chamber ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bissett, you mentioned yesterday that your American colleague, Ambassador Zimmerman, had told you that Mr. Baker had told the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Ante Markovic, that he would not consider inappropriate any use of the army in Slovenia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the federal government did send the federal police and the federal army into Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was this army answerable to; the federal authorities or the authorities of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would answer to the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to some questions concerning misinformation about the events in Yugoslavia during those years, you made a couple of points. Can you tell us why, from what you know, there was so much inaccurate information and misinformation about what was going on in Yugoslavia during those years?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, as I said yesterday, right from the very beginning it seemed that the -- the worldwide media took the position that Serbia and the Serbians were responsible for the break-up of Yugoslavia and that Croatia and Slovenia had broken away because they were frightened of Serbian plans for a Greater Serbia. That impression seemed to be reinforced when the media interpreted the attempt by the federal army to put down the secession of Slovenia. And as I said, the media did interpret that as the Serbia-dominated federal army attacking poor little Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do not cover ground that you've already gone over. Use the time profitably. On three occasions the ambassador has had to say, "As I said yesterday ..." Let's move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, you mentioned yesterday the role of Germany. Did you have any information as to the ways in which Germany supported Croatia, and how did you view the positions of Germany in the light of preserving peace and geopolitical relations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that? Is this a history lesson? Do not answer that. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a history lesson. I'm following up on what I received in the form of documents from the side opposite, namely wires sent by Ambassador Bissett.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that may be relevant, and the position of Germany in the light of preserving peace and geopolitical relations is of no interest to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Then tell us -- tell me what is of interest to you and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, in one of your cables, you say that I told you: "[In English] ... threats by Foreign Minister Genscher to recognise Croatia as example of German's 'heavy-handedness.'" [Interpretation] Are you aware of those German threats and the threats made by the German foreign minister at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that Foreign Minister Genscher had threatened to unilaterally recognise Croatia and Slovenia's independence, and it was common knowledge that Germany was pressuring other members of the European Community to -- to recognise both of the countries that were seceding. That was not a secret. It was quite well known. And Genscher himself wasn't -- did not try to hide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about the evolution of the position of other countries, especially EU countries, towards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not hear that. No, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me make this perfectly clear: You have spent 15 minutes, and you have not yet asked a question that's related to any of the charges in the indictment. If you continue this way, I will terminate the examination-in-chief. Don't waste the time of the Chamber. Don't waste the ambassador's time either. Bring the witness to evidence that is relevant to the indictment. We have had enough evidence on these background matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not really background. In the indictment and in all the evidence led by the other side, the leitmotif seems to be that the fear was caused among Serbs in Croatia by propaganda from Belgrade, and I wish to ask Ambassador Bissett, who spent precisely those years in Yugoslavia, in Belgrade, about this, because some claim that Serbs used their historical suffering through the centuries in order to justify crimes they committed at the end of the 20th century. I want to ask him what he knows about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But didn't he comment on that yesterday? He commented on that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he did in full, but if you consider that he already commented on that, I will not insist. I suppose that Ambassador Bissett is capable of assessing himself whether his brief comments of yesterday are sufficient or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll allow you to make a brief comment on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, yesterday you said: "The premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia by the European Union extended under intense German pressure in Maastricht in 1991, was a guarantee that the break-up of Yugoslavia would not be resolved by peaceful means. Once again, Western intervention had exacerbated and complicated a serious Balkan problem." That's a quotation from what you'd written. Now, that says it all, as far as I can see. There's nothing else to be explored. Why -- why this happened is irrelevant to this trial. The fact that it may have happened is what's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ambassador, a very brief response.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't think it was just the historical fact of the genocide that had taken place in 1941 that the Serbian population in Croatia were frightened of activities that were taking place after Mr. Tudjman's party won the election. I think there was also dismissal of Serbs from the public service of Croatia. There was harassment of Serbs. Many of them lost their flats. By -- even before 1993, I think roughly 300.000 Serbs had left Croatia. So they had reason, I think, to fear, quite apart from history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, do you know that Serbia's support to the Serbs of Krajina and the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina was interpreted and is interpreted here as my effort to create a Greater Serbia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about that? Was there indeed an objective held by me or the leadership of Serbia to create a Greater Serbia, which, according to what we were able to hear in this courtroom, could have been a reason to break up Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view, the idea that Serbia or yourself had entered into any sort of criminal conspiracy to establish a Greater Serbia is pure fantasy. I think the record speaks for itself that every attempt to negotiate a peace agreement and to stop the fighting and the violence, that you were personally involved in that. There were many initiatives taken by yourself, as well as by the international community, that, without your assistance, would have failed. And this goes right from the first Vance-Owen Plan, the Vance-Stoltenberg Plan, both plans which were subverted not by you or by the Serbian side but by others. And at Dayton itself there is no question that had you not been there, that the Dayton agreement would not have been signed, which finally brought peace to the warfare there. So I think the idea that you were attempting to establish a Greater Serbia is pure fantasy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 9 of your telegram that we considered yesterday, you quote my explanation for why -- for what I was advocating, what I was working for as regards the problems of Serbs in Croatia. You wrote in that paragraph: "[In English] He did, however, fully support autonomy for those areas of Croatia where Serbs made up predominant part of population; e.g., Krajina." What you wrote here, briefly, and we discussed it, namely what I was working for then, was that autonomy in case Croatia secedes from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm having trouble finding the right telegram here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's in tab 1, Mr. Bissett.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I -- as I recall it, it was related to the idea that if Croatia secede, that it could probably do so lawfully as long as some absolute guarantees were given to the Serbian population in Krajina and that they would have some form of autonomy and their civil and human rights protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bissett. At the relevant time you were following the events, including my actions and the actions taken by the authorities in Serbia. Did you find any indication that we had territorial ambitions against those republics?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any indication to the contrary, indication that we did not have any territorial claims?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in all of the proposals, the possible peace proposals, there was no suggestion that Serbia would gain territory from the settlements. It seemed to me very clear in all of these negotiations and peace plans that the one concern was the protection of the human rights and civil rights of the Serbian populations in Croatia where they were a majority and had lived for many hundreds of years, and for the Serbs later in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, from all I told you in our conversation on the 2nd of September and which is partially reflected in paragraph 10 of your cable, what was it that destroyed the unity of Yugoslavia? You say the advent of Slovenia's and Croatia's independence.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there's no question of what destroyed Yugoslavia. It was the decision by Croatia and Slovenia to secede from the federation. The unfortunate part of that secession was, as I recall, the federal Yugoslav constitution made provision for secession but only if the constituent nations were agreeable, and that was not the case. It wasn't important in Slovenia, but it was very important in Croatia where the Serbian population, via the constitution, were considered a constituent nation and any break-away or any secession would have had to have been done with their agreement. Therefore, it seems clear to me that both the separation of Slovenia and Croatia, and later Bosnia, were illegal and against the Yugoslav constitution. The fact that the separation -- the secession in Croatia and Slovenia were both done with violence I consider makes it even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able, even at that time, to see clearly enough the violent nature of secession that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Even by March of 1991, there had been armed conflict in parts of Croatia. There was fighting that had been -- that was -- had been breaking out in parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of establishing then what the role played by the Yugoslav People's Army was and what it strove for, faced with the situation of that kind, that is to say in this situation of conflict?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav national army was, of course, devoted and dedicated to the preservation of Yugoslavia, and I think it certainly assumed that one of its duties would be to put down armed secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, with respect to the events of which you were an eyewitness yourself, and according to the Croatia indictment and the Bosnian indictment against me, I, the members of the SFRY Presidency who were opposed to the secession, members of the top military echelons, the Serb leaders in Krajina and Bosnia have been termed as participants in a joint enterprise, criminal enterprise. Now, at that time when you were there, these strivings to preserve Yugoslavia and -- was it a joint criminal enterprise or was it a constitutional obligation? How did you see things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to comment on. Those are legal issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't ask the witness any legal questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, you were in Yugoslavia doing your job when the Vance Plan was adopted. Who, from whom, and why were the United Nations peace forces supposed to protect?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to protect the Serb population in the Serbian areas of Croatia, in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And whose duty was it to protect that population from that same source of jeopardy before the United Nations forces arrived?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, it was the EC monitors, who were there prior to the Vance Plan being implemented, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember whether there were any difficulties over the adoption of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the Vance Plan, yes, I think there was initial difficulties when, as I recall, we were all very pleased -- that is the diplomatic corps in Belgrade were pleased to know that the plan was going to be adopted because it was the first real effort to stop the bloodshed, but at last minute it seemed that the Croatian -- sorry, the Serbian Prime Minister, Babic, backed off and refused to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember from those days what my reactions to that were?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember you were upset that Babic had -- who had first agreed to sign and then changed his mind, I remember you were upset about that and had an article in the front page of the Politika newspaper condemning Babic. I think as a result of your pressure, Babic finally did sign and the plan went ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you that article of mine that you mentioned a moment ago? And it is number 2. Not in the tab. It's not tab 2, it's just under number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, gentlemen, that is Exhibit 352, tab 79, exhibits already tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should just like to ask you something with respect to that letter of mine that you mentioned. Do you remember what I wrote?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember what you wrote, but I have it in front of me now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the usher put it on the ELMO. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did this letter refer to anybody else except for Babic? And would you look at page 6, towards the very end of the translation, because of course you have the English text before you. That very last portion highlighted in darker letters: "Serbia will not stop helping the people of Krajina ..."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- not in reading this, but do you remember generally whether this letter referred to any other person except Babic, who at that time had refused the plan which he had agreed to beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, take a look at the previous paragraph. What does it say there? Would you read it out, please. "It has become obvious ..." That one.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has become obvious for quite some time that you have been creating an impression among the citizens of Krajina that you make your decisions and take your positions following agreement with the Serbian leadership. Thus, I want the citizens of Krajina to know that this is not true."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, from those times and from following events, how many such abuses there were, that is to say that something was linked to the leadership of Serbia when it wasn't true, as it was in this case when I have to state publicly that it was not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't really recall other -- other, as you say, abuses that were linked to your leadership when it wasn't true. If you're -- if you're specifically mentioning that other people were publicly saying that they had discussions with you and you said such-and-such, I can't recall any of those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I asked you, whether you remember. If you don't remember, we can move on. It isn't the most important thing now. In paragraph 11 of your telegram, you say that in talking to me, you were interested in learning about the situation with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that I told you of the risks involved, the risks that a possible secession would create. Do you remember that part of our conversation? You sent out a brief information about it in paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, because of course it was the fear of everyone, again among the members of the diplomatic corps and others, that fighting could spill over into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we were interested to know if Bosnia declared its independence what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the assessment made that we discussed, and do you consider that to have been the right assessment?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I think it simply confirmed the views of most observers at the time, that if there was an attempt for Bosnia to gain independence without the agreement of the Serbs and the Croatian population, there would be bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you say something about that. Where I saw the solution lying "[In English] ... to join in some form of federalism or union with Serbia and Montenegro." Do you remember whether at that time my actions and the actions of the government in Serbia confirmed this assertion that we considered this kind of solution to be desirable?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. I think there was at least one, maybe two attempts to enter into some form of agreement with the Bosnian president that would avoid the bloodshed and keep Bosnia-Herzegovina within the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember those attempts or do you just know that such attempts were made? I'm not going to enumerate them if you can't remember them. You said there were several attempts.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall -- I can't recall the details of it, but there was an initiative taken, as I recall, sometime in the summer of 1991, in August, where Serbia and Montenegro - I'm not sure if Macedonia was present - and you invited Mr. Izetbegovic, President Izetbegovic, to come and work out a form of an arrangement that would entail Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining in a new federation. I also think the major effort was, of course, made in Lisbon in March of 1992 when the Portuguese foreign minister, Cutileiro, arranged to have the three constituent parts of Bosnia - Serbs, Croats and Muslims - sign an agreement that would have worked out some form of cantonment in Bosnia, and those -- that effort was seen by -- certainly by myself and many of my diplomatic colleagues as a major breakthrough and a last-ditch effort to prevent the violence from spreading in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I have your comments, please, to what you wrote in paragraph 12 of your telegram. You say here: "... expressed view that the majority of Muslims [In English] in Bosnia and Herzegovina realised that they must reach an accord with the Serbs so that both peoples could live in harmony." [Interpretation] At the end of that paragraph: "[In English] He expressed the view that a small minority of Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina dreamed of creating a Muslim state in Europe but doubted that many took this seriously." [Interpretation] Do you remember that part of our conversation and how developments followed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. And I also recall that, of course, there were thousands and thousands of people in Bosnia, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats who were marching for peace, who were frightened that war could break out there, and I think that what you said probably has come to pass, although it turned out that it wasn't a small minority of Muslims that voted for independence, but I think at the time you gave me that information I thought that it confirmed with my own views that most of the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not want bloodshed and violence and were frightened that it was going to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your telegram, you say that I told you that I had hoped that it would be the Yugoslavs themselves who would be able, without outside intervention, to solve their problems. To the best of your knowledge and according to your experience, does that confirm the correctness of those hopes or the falsity of them?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 14, I'll quote that portion for you from that paragraph. We were discussing the kind of foreign mediators that should come, and it says: "[In English] Such being the case, it was fundamentally important that the mediators be knowledgeable and above all impartial." [Interpretation] So I'm asking you now, to the best of your knowledge, those foreign mediators in the Yugoslav crisis, did they have the necessary knowledge and impartiality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said yesterday that I think that the European Community mediators already started off with a bias against Serbia, and in -- although they were sending observers in to prevent the fighting between Serbs and Croatians in Croatia, they knew at the time, as did everyone else, that the Croatian army had at that time occupied all of Western Herzegovina, and yet nothing was said about that and sanctions were applied to Serbia, not equally to Croatia. So I think there was bias from the very beginning, that the interpretation was that Serbia was responsible for the break-up and the violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, in document 1, which is an exhibit in these proceedings -- that's not important for you, but anyway, there's a report there by the UN Secretary-General, dated the 30th of May, 1992. That is to say -- or, rather, is that -- what you said a moment ago about bias and the presence of -- or, rather, the existence of this, was that something that the United Nations was aware of as to actually happening within the international community and what was actually going on?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have it on the screen, please, before evidence is adduced about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in March of 1991, I think it was fairly common knowledge and reported in most of the media that the Croatian army was in Western Herzegovina. In the document that you've produced - I've had the opportunity of reading it - it's a report to the Secretary-General, it does indicate, I think pretty clearly, that the Croatians had not withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does it say that the JNA had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you explain then this: The Croatian army didn't leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had practically previously not existed, whereas the Yugoslav People's Army, which had been there for 70 years, did withdraw? So that is the fact. Sanctions are introduced against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- or, rather, Serbia and Montenegro, whereas they kept quiet on the situation going on on the other side, which was quite different. Do you have an explanation for that now, or perhaps did you have one then?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation. But it simply does, I think, prove that there was bias on the part of some of the international organisations that were trying to bring peace to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your telegram, you say: "I asked Milosevic if he sincerely felt that there could be a settlement [In English] of these terrible ethnic struggles so rooted in history and bloodshed. He replied optimistically by saying that once the Serb minority problem in Croatia was settled - and it was in the interest of Croatia to do this - then sensible and effective negotiation could begin." [Interpretation] Was that then and now, when you look back, the way to move forward towards resolving the problem?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was. And again, I think I said that yesterday, that if there could have been a settlement of the Serbian minority problem in Croatia, then most of the problems and the great tragedy that overtook Yugoslavia could have been prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the steps made by the Serbian authorities and my own steps? Did they show that we stand behind a stance of this kind, the kind of position that I explained to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's -- that's been clear, that you yourself and indeed the official Serbian position was that unless satisfactory protection can be given to the minorities in Croatia, that successful resolution of the problem could not come about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you ask so many leading questions that one tires of bringing it to your attention. That was a very leading question, and it got the response which you -- which was embedded in the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what a leading question is here if I'm quoting from what Ambassador Bissett wrote in his telegram and then I ask him whether the position was in conformity with a stance of that kind to the best of his knowledge. And he's not a minor for me to ask him leading questions and for me to elicit an answer that I want to hear by doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The proper question should have been, "What did they show?" Just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what you wrote, we were discussing security for the Serb minority and then later on negotiations. So those were two points. Security was achieved through the implementation of the Vance Plan. And now I'm going to ask you, did the negotiations ever come about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiations for solving the problems for the Serbian minority in Croatia, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Did the negotiations take place?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did take place. There were negotiations. Unfortunately, they did not -- they did not succeed in the long term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what, in your opinion, was the cause of the failure of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The failure of the negotiations, there's different interpretations of that. I can only give you my own opinion. I think in the Vance-Owen Plan, and later on the other Vance-Stoltenberg Plans failed because of primarily outside influence by the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection to what you've just said and mentioning Cutileiro's plan to touch upon the Bosnian crisis now and focus on that for a while, in addition to these attempts and agreements between the Serbs and Muslims, do you know about the relationship of the Serb side in Bosnia towards the peace efforts being made and principally the plan you just mentioned which was popularly known as the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember it very well because it seemed to be a last-ditch effort to prevent bloodshed, and the -- Cutileiro had gathered the three leaders, Karadzic, Izetbegovic, and Boban, to Lisbon, and they worked out a satisfactory settlement and all three leaders signed it. It seemed a time for rejoicing because it was a solution to a very difficult problem, and it appeared to be a satisfactory settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the general standpoint taken by your colleagues among the diplomatic corps in Belgrade, or was it only your own standpoint?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think it was generally acknowledged by certainly the greater part of the diplomatic corps as a great relief; that if the Bosnian problem could be settled, then the Croatian and the Serbian ongoing dispute would probably fall in place. So everyone was relieved, because I think everyone knew that if a referendum was to take place in Bosnia and independence given to Izetbegovic, it would be civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a little while ago you said that all three leaders, Karadzic, Izetbegovic, and Boban, signed the Cutileiro Plan. What happened after that? Do you have any personal knowledge of what ensued afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. My neighbour, the United States ambassador, Mr. Zimmerman, flew to Sarajevo and had a meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. Following that meeting, Izetbegovic rescinded his agreement to the Cutileiro Plan, withdrew his signature. Mr. Zimmerman has written in his book that when he arrived in Sarajevo to discuss the plan with Izetbegovic, Izetbegovic expressed regret that he had signed it. Mr. Zimmerman then said, "Well, if you didn't want to sign it, why don't you withdraw your signature and go ahead with your referendum? If you do that, the United States will immediately recognise your independence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you written a book, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is Mr. Zimmerman's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I was asking if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must be one of the very few.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't plan to write one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, was Zimmerman's role well known, the one he mentions in passing in his book? Was it known to you and other members of the diplomatic corps, at least those among the Western diplomats?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know what had transpired between Mr. Zimmerman and Mr. Izetbegovic. We suspected something had happened to make Mr. Izetbegovic change his mind, but Mr. Zimmerman never discussed the matter personally with me other than having said that Izetbegovic wasn't happy with the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned the referendum. What did you know about this referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what I knew about it is that if it took place, it was highly likely the Serbian population would opt out of the referendum, that they considered it to be illegal, and that if the referendum went ahead, Izetbegovic would win it, would be granted independence, and civil war would be the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the second telegram you have here. It's the one dated the 21st of March, 1991. Have you found it, Mr. Bissett?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 4. Towards the end, in the last two sentences of point 4, but you can put it aside now and I will read out to you paragraph 94 of the Croatia indictment, where it says that: "In March 1991 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Paragraph 99, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "-- the members of the Presidency ... resigned on ... [In English] 16th of March, 1991, Slobodan Milosevic, in his capacity as president of the Republic of Serbia, declared that Yugoslavia was finished and that Serbia would no longer be bound by decisions of the Federal Presidency." [Interpretation] You have my address in English in the documents before you. Can you find that speech? It's in tab 51 of the exhibits we had with Branko Kostic. Look at page 2 of the text in English and what was used here: "Serbia would no longer be bound by decisions of the Federal Presidency. "[In English] In light of the situation, I wish to announce that the Republic of Serbia will not be recognising any decision of the Presidency of SFRY because any such decision would be illegitimate under the present circumstances." So is it illegitimacy under the present circumstances or what it says here, "no longer"? Do you remember that as you discussed it with me? How long did those present circumstances last, the ones mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't last very long. A matter of a few days, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here in your telegram, on page 4, at the end: "[In English] Milosevic added Serb Assembly may or may not accept Jovic's resignation, but by 21st of March ... there should be Serb representative in Federal Presidency." [Interpretation] As a foreign diplomat, the chief of your country's mission, were you able to conclude in any way that Serbia would no longer participate in the Presidency or recognise its decisions? As it says here, "Serbia would no longer be bound by decisions ..."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think as a result of the meeting with you, you clarified the position and made it clear that by the 21st of March, Serbia would be back in the Presidency. I might add to that that prior to the meeting, our meeting, there was a great deal of confusion about Jovic's resignation and about your appearance on television. It was turbulent times, and there was a great deal of tension, and many diplomats, including myself, were uncertain as to what was happening with Jovic's resignation. So it was a difficult time and a time of crisis, because it seemed that there might be some effort made to -- at the last minute to try and stop Croatia and Slovenia from seceding. A lot of misinterpretation of your television appearance. And so it was with some degree of relief that when we met with you, you were able to explain that Serbia had withdrawn temporarily, decide whether you should or should not accept Jovic's resignation, but at any rate you would be back in the Presidency by the 21st, and that happened, as you predicted it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, for the record I have to note that the passage appears on page 3, not 4, in the English telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my copy it's page 4 point 4, but it may be different in the copy you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that we have clarified this part, but now let's try and clarify the first element contained here in paragraph 99 of the indictment, where it says: "Slobodan Milosevic declared that Yugoslavia was finished." Would you please now read on page 1 of the English translation what it says here in this passage. It's a subtitle from a newspaper. "[In English] As to Serbia, she has always been in favour of Yugoslavia --" [Interpretation] Can you find it on page 1 of the translation?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] -- and has never tried to hide it. Always in favour of Yugoslavia and has never tried it -- to hide it. It is with profound conviction and a sense of pride that she says this publicly now." [Interpretation] And then at the end of the following passage: "[In English] Yugoslavia does exist, and it may not be annulled by means of unilateral enactments and the policy of fait accompli because the real interests, the achieved freedoms and democratic heritage and the strength of the peoples living there are guarantee of its survival and successful development." [Interpretation] You had an opportunity at the time while you were there to see me making this speech, to hear me, to understand this. Is this beyond dispute?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think -- I think it was -- you made it quite clear in your speech that the withdrawal was temporary and that you still -- that Yugoslavia was still existing and that Serbia fully supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think anyone can draw this conclusion stated here, that I declared that Yugoslavia was finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he can't say that. He can't say that, Mr. Milosevic, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what I said at the time, and you were then the Canadian ambassador in Belgrade, could you or any colleague of yours in any way get the idea that this was activity aimed against the existence of Yugoslavia or declaring that Yugoslavia no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Certainly it seemed quite clear to me what -- what your intent was, that you were still supporting the concept and idea of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me just take a look at this paragraph 103 from the same Croatia indictment, which says: "[In English] Slobodan Milosevic's calls for the union of all Serbs in one state ..." [Interpretation] I'll skip over "... coincided with those agitating for a 'Greater Serbia.'" My call for all Serbs in one state. Please read the middle of the passage on page 1 of the translation from my speech made at the time. What does it say? Or maybe we can even read the whole passage so as not to get anything out of context, to avoid objections that we are pulling a segment out of context. It's the passage where I say: "With the obstruction of work of the Presidency." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] ... on the part of those pursuing the policy of disintegration of the country, the plan to break up Yugoslavia has entered its final phase. This plan is being implemented to the detriment of the vital interests of Serbian people in both Serbia and Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] And this is what I wish to emphasise, why I'm quoting this: "[In English] In place of a democratic federation which should provide Serbian people and the other peoples with a peaceful life, that is in joint state but that is one state --" [Interpretation] I say in one state in the Serbian -- "[In English] on an equal footing, these forces of the anti-Serbian coalition have planned the outbreak -- the break-up of Yugoslavia and are now trying to see this through. Yugoslavia does exist, and it may not be annulled by means of unilateral enactment and the policy of fait accompli because the interests ..." and so on and so on. [Interpretation] That's the whole passage. Is there any mention here of a call for all Serbs to join in one state or does it mention a democratic federation which should provide the Serbian people and the other peoples with a peaceful life in "[In English] one state on an equal footing"? [Interpretation] Can one say that what is stated here was actually a call by Slobodan Milosevic for the union of all Serbs in one state?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Yugoslavia a state in which all Serbs, Croats, and south southern -- South Slav Muslims lived as well as Macedonians and Slovenians? Was that the state we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment. I'm passing over something I can't find now. Look at the beginning of paragraph 5 of that same telegram. You talk about my views on ways of solving the Kosovo problem. Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] Milosevic elaborated on number of points at ambassadors lunch, including Serbia's democratic tradition since 1918. Kosovo's demographic pressures could be resolved by economic progress. In meantime, Serb government will not allow that part of Serbia to be annexed by [sic] Albania ..." [Interpretation] I'm quoting this for the sake of correctness, but does it say here [In English] could be resolved by what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By economic progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now put -- just a moment. I'll now put a few more questions to you about the article we've already used in this book by the Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies, the article you authored. And it refers to Kosovo. It's on page 56, the second passage from the bottom of the page. Please read it out - it's from your article - and then I'll ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Given the experience of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia, it is little wonder that the Albanians in Kosovo realised the most effective way to gain independence was to take up arms and resort to violence. This had been the formula for success before and there was every reason to expect it would work again. Indeed, given the successful public relations campaign that had been waged against President Milosevic and the Serbs, and the record of human rights violations in Kosovo, it was inevitable that Kosovo would be the next part of Yugoslavia to break away."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you think about the Rambouillet agreement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I thought the Rambouillet agreement was an attempt by the United States, primarily, to force Yugoslavia to accept unreasonable terms. And I am also convinced that when the initial terms of Rambouillet were accepted by the Serbian side, the Americans at the last moment attached an Appendix B to the agreement, which called for the permission of NATO troops to enter all of Yugoslavia, not just Kosovo, and as well to have a referendum on independence within three years. I think it's generally known that that Appendix B was attached knowing that any President of Serbia would be unable to accept those terms, and it was a deliberate attempt, I think, to lead to the bombing of Yugoslavia. I am not alone in thinking this. Lord Gilbert, who I think was assistant permanent secretary of the British Department of Defence, in an address to the British House of Commons in July of 2000, in effect said that Rambouillet was a provocation which would allow NATO to use force to try and resolve the Kosovo problem. Mr. Rubin, of the United States, in an article in the Observer - I don't have the dates - as well has admitted this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, after Rambouillet, the aggression started against Yugoslavia that they referred to as the bombing. In your insight into that situation and in your public appearances, did you appraise -- did you see that as a war crime or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he see what as a war crime? He can't comment on -- the characterisation of anything as a war crime is not a matter for the witness. Mr. Milosevic, you seem to be searching for questions. If you are at the end of the examination-in-chief, then let us stop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am close to the end of my examination-in-chief, but I'm not searching for questions. I will rephrase this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, how did you see that attack that followed immediately after Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already described my reaction to it. I thought it was a violation of international law, I thought it was a violation of the United Nations Charter, and for me personally, it was also shocking to find that it was a violation of everything that NATO had stood for since its inception. NATO was originally a defensive organisation. As I said, its Article 1 of its treaty said that NATO would never use violence in the resolution of international disputes, indeed would not threaten to use force. So that was my reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your article, in the book published by the Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies, on page 57 you wrote -- please look at the last but one paragraph on page 57. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you write here?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "President Clinton told the American people that the war was being fought for humanitarian reasons and to contain the fighting so that it would not imperil or destabilise the rest of the Balkans. The bombing was necessary, he said, to stop the atrocities being committed there. This was justification for the violation of Yugoslav sovereignty. In the same vein, Canadian ministers of national defence and foreign affairs assured their citizens that the war was being fought to stop ethnic cleansing. It is, of course, a matter of record that the vast majority of Kosovo Albanians were forced out of Kosovo after the bombing, not before it. Nevertheless, these ministers were not alone in heralding the war as ushering in a new era of diplomacy. Humanitarian reasons --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So NATO leaders stated publicly that this was designed to stop ethnic cleansing, and you mentioned here the notorious fact that it was after the bombing. It is in cursive here in the text; after the bombing, not before it. How did you see those explanations by NATO leaders? What is your assessment? And finally, what do you believe was the real reason for the NATO bombing of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that's not a matter -- we're not interested in that, Mr. Milosevic. Let me see whether you can ask the witness any of these questions. NATO leaders stated publicly this was designed to stop ethnic cleansing. What did you want to ask, anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did ask. They did state that, and Mr. Bissett is saying quite clearly that the wave of refugees happened after the bombing, not before. So what was going on really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm on record saying and writing frequently that I think the real reason that NATO bombed Yugoslavia was not at all because of anything that was happening in Kosovo, but it was an opportunity for NATO, on the eve of its 50th birthday, to demonstrate, particularly to the European countries, that NATO was still a viable and necessary organisation. NATO had been under attack and criticised, wondering why it continued to exist, this powerful military force, when the Warsaw Pact armies had long ago gone home. And the situation in Kosovo was ideal, an ideal opportunity for NATO to demonstrate it was still a useful force. That's my own feeling, and it's shared by many observers, but it's an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would make NATO out to be very cynical and opportunistic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I think that might have been proven on the 50th birthday party, where Mr. President Clinton announced a completely new role for NATO which he said would permit it to act out of area. In other words, NATO would now, from now on, be allowed to intervene anywhere in the world whenever it felt that it was necessary to do so. That was not the terms of the original treaty, and I would have thought if the terms of that treaty were to be altered, the treaty would have to be renegotiated and signed by all members, but again that's my personal view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ambassador, you were a career diplomat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next page in your article, 58, the last paragraph, since you mentioned Clinton. What did you write here?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The US-led attack on Yugoslavia was designed to improve President Clinton's public image and restore credibility to NATO, whose existence since the end of the Cold War was in jeopardy. This was the real agenda of the NATO war. In terms of Balkan history, it is an old agenda. Traditionally, Western intervention in the Balkans has proven to be disastrous. From the Congress of Berlin to both World Wars, the Western powers have intervened in the Balkans for their own selfish policy objectives. These aims have in the end --" Sorry: "These aims have had little relevance to the issues affecting the peoples of the Balkan countries. What was true of the past has proven true again in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then there is an explanation to be found in the next paragraph, where you say: "Because of the demonic image the Western media had already created ..." Would you please read this.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Because of the demonic image the Western media had already created of Slobodan Milosevic, it was not difficult for him to be blamed for committing outrageous atrocities in Kosovo. In fact, prior to the bombing, the total casualties in Kosovo, Serb and Albanian, did not reach beyond 2000, which by any standard was not cause for military intervention. Nevertheless, NATO needed its war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: NATO proclaimed that the bombing of Yugoslavia, and primarily Serbia, was a great victory. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree that it was a great victory. I think it set a very dangerous precedent. It now would appear that NATO has taken upon itself the right to intervene wherever it so chooses, without regard to international law and without regard whatsoever to the United Nations, and I think that's a sad commentary on an organisation that was designed to defend democracy and the freedoms and not engage in violence to resolve international disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you think about Resolution 1244 that ended the war.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that 1244 was a satisfactory solution to the problem. Unfortunately, it doesn't appear to have been fully complied with. 1244 guaranteed the civil rights and protection of all people in Kosovo of whatever ethnic origin. The first results of 1244 was the ethnic cleansing of the non-Albanian population from Kosovo, and this was done under the eyes of some 30 or 40.000 NATO troops. 1244 guaranteed that the religious sites in Kosovo would be protected, but we've seen that over 130 Orthodox churches have been either dynamited and blasted to the ground or burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this evidence relates to a period not relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the entire context is very relevant. If you want to see the whole picture, you cannot neglect this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, you were there for a while. In another period you followed all that happened in the 1990s in the former Yugoslavia. How can you explain this great bloodshed and ethnic cleansing and violence in general that happened on all sides in the region? Did you write and speak about this? Did you have discussions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How -- Mr. Milosevic, I think we are now in the period of diminishing returns. His explanation of the bloodshed and the ethnic cleansing is not going to help us very much. If you don't have any more questions, just let us move on to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you do not allow the witness to answer this question, let me ask another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, in view of all that you witnessed in the years when the conflict started in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and in the years when you followed it from afar, who do you think is primarily responsible for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not allowing that. That is a decision that we will make on the basis of the evidence presented to us. You're in the area now, the period of sweeping generalisations. I take it you have concluded. Mr. Nice, please begin. There is a tab to be -- we will admit tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Trinidad and Tobago was the embassy you went to first, was it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a High Commission in the Commonwealth, an embassy position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then back to Canada and then two years or a little more in Belgrade. Sent there by Prime Minister Mulroney, and at the end of your turn of office or tour of duty, I think you pleaded with the Foreign Minister Barbara McDougall, is it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To stay on while other embassies were withdrawing their ambassadors, and you stayed on longer than any of the others, no doubt with the consent of Mr. Mulroney.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Based largely in Belgrade, doing your two years there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I also had responsibility as ambassador for Albania, as I mentioned, and also Bulgaria, so I made trips to both those countries fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As an ambassador, or former ambassador, you can have a reasonable expectation, can you not, Mr. Bissett, that your words will be attended to and accorded some weight?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think that with that expectation there comes the duty to check your facts?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You published a little between 1992 and 1999, but the real trigger for your life as a publicist was the bombing, wasn't it, because the bombing was something you absolutely disagreed with, as you made clear today.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And since then you have published widely.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've written quite a number of articles, yes. I haven't written a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've expressed views not only on the role of NATO, which you've repeated, but when you were first called here as a witness and this Court had imposed a counsel on this accused, you sent a letter saying that you thought this was a political court rather than a juridical body operating in the interests of justice and in truth. You said that it had already, this Tribunal, determined the accused's guilt and that the proceedings had the characteristics of a Stalinist show-trial. Now, those were your views then. Are they still your views?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not my views now, not all of that. I was reacting to the fact that Mr. Milosevic was not going to be allowed to represent himself, and I thought that was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did that support -- that's why I asked you about checking your facts. Did that support your assertion that this was a political court? The fact that the three Judges made a judicial decision in the course of their duties, does that make this a political court, please, Mr. Bissett?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I was the only one who was critical of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, I think the question was easy enough to answer. Does the fact that a court, through its Judges, makes a decision with which you disagree make this a political court?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it did. It certainly added to some of my previous views that I've also written about the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may come and have a look at those, but just so that we can understand exactly how strong it may be your emotions are, you as a former ambassador, with access to the leading politicians and diplomats of your day, have on your website today - because I'm reading it - a likening of the present Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte, to Hitler's favoured prosecutor Roland Fiesler, who presided over the trial of those involved in the July 20th plot. Do you think that, in your position, that is a responsible publication to put out for the world at large to read?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I put it out. It may be considered irresponsible by some but it may not be considered by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You really -- we are concerned here, Mr. Bissett, as you will well understand, with a ten-year history that involves the consequences of extravagant expressions of opinion by ethnic groups supported by individuals. Do you think likening the Prosecutor here in that way is a responsible thing for a man in your position to do?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's not just this Prosecutor that you have attacked. I'm going to hand you, please, if I can, a selection of your material on your website. I'm only going to take you through a few examples, but I'd ask you, over the break, to cast your eye over the others and to confirm that they are indeed opinions you have published. Now, looking at this document, as the footnote reveals, unless otherwise stated, they are quotations from your own website, and the first one is the letter sent when you were first asked to come here as a witness. But on that same page -- on the first page, page 1, I just draw to your attention this: You said of this Tribunal that it had lost all credibility by its bias in favour of NATO patrons. It had become a political organ of NATO. Its decision to issue indictments against Milosevic in the middle of the bombing campaign was a blatant attempt to gain public support for the bombing. After all, who would not support punitive action being taken against a nation headed by an accused war criminal? And with in mind that that relates to the former Prosecutor Justice Louise Arbour, would you go to page 2, please. The first bullet point, new bullet point there. You make various allegations against the former Prosecutor, and then you say this: "There seems little doubt the announcement was timed to bolster sagging public support for the bombing. After all, who would dare oppose the bombing of a country whose leader had been indicted as war criminal? That Louise Arbour would violate the Tribunal's policy is not surprising. Her appointment to the Tribunal was conditional upon receiving the approval of Madeleine Albright." Now, you are quite clearly, in public domain, making allegations of corrupt practices by a woman who happens now to be a United Nations commissioner. Would you please tell us what your evidence in support of those publicly made allegations is, Mr. Bissett.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been told by international lawyers that it was the policy of the Tribunal not to announce or publicise those that were going to be indicted, yet after the bombing of Kosovo had commenced, Louise Arbour, the former Chief Prosecutor, did publicly announce the indictment of President Milosevic, was seen in Kosovo before what was alleged to be mass graves, allegedly of Kosovo victims of crimes, and I thought that was probably inappropriate. The fact that the United States -- it was through United States pressure that the court was established by the Security Council and the fact that Madeleine Albright did interview Louise Arbour, I have my own reasons for suspecting that her appointment to the Tribunal was conditional upon getting Madeleine Albright's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know -- have you bothered to research what the process for issuing and confirming an indictment is in this court?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you think that the material you have referred to is sufficient to make this sort of public allegation on a website, do you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously I did because I published it on my website.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me this: Have you made any attempt to contact Justice Louise Arbour about your allegations, to check with her, to ask her, to verify from any source the sort of material you put out?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at one more example of your decision-making process and then I'll return to what you've given in evidence. On the same page, you deal with Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please ask Mr. Nice and Ambassador Bissett to observe the pause. They speak the same language, and it's very difficult for interpreters to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask both Ambassador Bissett and Mr. Nice to observe the pause between question and answer in the interest of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the interpreters are having a problem and I hadn't heard it, I apologise to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same page you deal with Racak, and I'm only concerned with this not for your conclusion but for your reasoning processes. "At the centre of the indictment against Milosevic was the infamous 'Racak massacre.'" You set out the allegation. "Madeleine Albright has described the 'Racak massacre' as the galvanising event leading to the air war ..." You then say: "The final report, published last week by the Finnish forensic experts who examined the bodies of the alleged victims, confirms what many suspected at the time, that there were no evidence to show the bodies discovered in the shallow trench by United States General William Walker were executed at close range." And you then go on to say this: "It seems the victims were armed members of the KLA who were killed in the fighting that had taken place in the hills above Racak the day before. Their bodies had been placed in the trench to simulate a massacre. This would suggest that at least some of the evidence against Milosevic presented by the United States to the Tribunal to support his indictment has been fabricated." Is that still your view?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is still my view about Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it? Well, help me, please: Have you spoken to any of the survivors from the gully in Racak of their experience?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any of the other people in Racak village who survived?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you sought to review the evidence that those people have given in this court?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen some of the evidence given in this court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you sought to review it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to review it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the evidence of international observers who spoke of what happened at Racak?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You disregard all that evidence, do you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't disregard it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you -- have you examined and considered the forensic scientific evidence in this case, and there is a great deal of it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've certainly read some of the reports of the scientific evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, please, Mr. Bissett, if people are killed in a gully - if - in execution by people standing at the side of the gully, mowing them down, where would you expect to find the bullets that killed the people; in the gully or on the bank?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would expect to find them in the bodies of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the gully. Where would you expect to find the spent cartridge cases if they had been mown down in execution by people standing on a bank?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know where the bullets and cartridges were found in respect of the gully?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've heard reports from German reporters who were around the trench shortly after, the day after the alleged massacre, that there were no empty cartridges found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you haven't followed the evidence in sufficient detail to know that there is in fact evidence of bullets and cartridge cases being found in exactly those places?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would that perhaps change your mind?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think if the forensic evidence could prove that the people were shot at close range and that the empty shells were around the bank and there was no evidence of fabrication, it would probably change my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you put out material - and we may look at some more, we may not - you put out material favourable to the Serb side trusting almost everything favourable to them that you hear, don't you? You don't look at things in detail and you don't listen to --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't publish everything in favour of the Serbs, but I will certainly admit that most of my writings have been prompted by the view that the Serbs have been demonised as a people and that this has been guilt by association and has had a dreadfully bad impact on the people of Serbia and the recovery from the war. I have not intended to defend NATO's actions or to defend anyone other than the Serbs and the Serbian people, because I felt they were unable to do so themselves, they had been demonised so badly by the public media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you accept -- what was it, in the course of those two years in Belgrade, occasionally going to Macedonia and Albania, was it in those two years that you developed this sympathy for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before that, was it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was after the accusations that -- made by the media and by others that the Serbs were -- were responsible for the break-up of Yugoslavia and were responsible for all of the crimes that ensued following the conflict there. It was then that I began to feel an obligation to point out that it was not the Serbs or Serbia who broke up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's your opinion, of course. You recognise that --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- there are many with a contrary view. And your opinion is based on what, a few meetings with this accused?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a few meetings with this accused; by the facts that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I was going to list things. First of all, you had a few meetings with this accused. A couple, was it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had probably four or five meetings with President Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Open source material that you received in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, open source material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Contact with your own staff and what they found?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And other discussions with other people in the diplomatic community at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And open source reading since?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it wasn't all open source material in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I can accept that, as a diplomat, you have access to other material. But it sounds - but correct me if I'm wrong - that you were never at one of the scenes of alleged criminal acts, were you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You never spoke, so far as you've said so far, to survivors of alleged criminal acts, scenes, have you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us a number of things about 1970 -- 1991. Before you arrived in 1989, we have heard from President Kucan of Slovenia that at a Central Committee meeting on the 30th of January of 1989 -- just -- he gave evidence to the effect that this accused said that things would have to be changed that cannot be changed institutionally, because people don't like them or because they lasted too long, will be changed uninstitutionally; i.e., expressing at that meeting a willingness to use uninstitutional or non-institutional means to achieve results. That fits, I imagine, with your understanding of the man, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, reformulate the question. It's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he prepared, in your judgement, to act outside the law, outside the proper role of the institutions when he judged it necessary?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
